To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) commitment of human keratinocytes to differentiation is a highly regulated process controlled by a network of protein dephosphorylating enzymes (phosphatases); (2) the activity of these phosphatases is regulated in time (i.e., they are up- or downregulated in the course of differentiation) and in space (i.e., their expression is spatially restricted in the epidermis); (3) this phosphatase network is inherently unstable, and thus
(i) a phosphatase network regulates commitment in human epidernis, and (ii) this phosphatase network is auto-regulatory and spatially regulated.
A protein phosphatase signalling network controls the duration and stability of the commitment state in human keratinocytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that regulate the transition of epidermal cells from stem cell to differentiated state.
the regulation of cell fate in epidermal stem cells.
the mechanisms of commitment in human skin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the protein phosphatase networks controls the temporal and the spatial dynamics of differentiation.
